title: Jade Emperor
description: Type of god in Chinese culture
wiki_lead:
In the myths and folk religion of Chinese culture, the Jade Emperor or Yudi is one of the representations of the primordial god.
In Taoist theology, he is the assistant of Yuanshi Tianzun, who is one of the Three Pure Ones, the three primordial emanations of the Tao. However, some Taoists in history were skeptical of his benevolence because his buildings and infrastructure in heaven and earth were sometimes seen as interfering with the many natural laws or dao.
He is often identified with Śakra in Chinese Buddhist cosmology and identified with Yu the Great in Chinese mythology.
The Jade Emperor is known by many names, including Yu; Heavenly Grandfather (Chinese: 天公, romanized: Tiāngōng), which originally meant "Heavenly Duke" (and which is used by commoners); the Jade Lord; the Highest Emperor; and Great Emperor of Jade (玉皇上帝, Yu Huang Shangdi, or 玉皇大帝, Yu Huang Dadi).

Chinese mythology

There are many stories in Chinese mythology involving the Jade Emperor. He can also be regarded as a traditional figure among the White Lotus Societies.


Origin
It was said that Jade Emperor was originally the crown prince of the kingdom of Pure Felicity and Majestic Heavenly Lights and Ornaments. At birth, he emitted a wondrous light that filled the entire kingdom. When he was young, he was kind, intelligent and wise. He devoted his entire childhood to helping the needy (the poor and suffering, the deserted and single, the hungry and disabled). Furthermore, he showed respect and benevolence to both men and creatures.
After his father died, he ascended the throne. He made sure that everyone in his kingdom found peace and contentment. After that, he told his ministers that he wished to cultivate Tao on the Bright and Fragrant Cliff.
After 17,501,750 eons, each eon lasting for 129,600 years (3602 years), he attained Golden Immortality. After another one hundred million years of cultivation, he finally became the Jade Emperor. (Using the given figures, this period before his becoming the Jade Emperor lasted for a total of about 327.000.000.327.000.000 years.)


Vanquishing evil
One of the myths describes how the Jade Emperor became the monarch of all the deities in heaven. It is one of the few myths in which the Jade Emperor shows his power.
At the beginning of time, the earth was a very difficult place to live, much harsher than it is now. People had to deal with a variety of monstrous beings, and they did not have many gods to protect them; in addition, many powerful demons were defying the immortals of heaven. The Jade Emperor was an ordinary immortal who roamed the earth helping as many people as he could. He was saddened because his powers could only ease the suffering of humans. He retreated to a mountain cave to cultivate his Tao. He passed 3,200 trials, each trial lasting about 3 million years.
On earth at this time, a powerful, evil entity had the ambition to conquer the immortals and gods in heaven and proclaim sovereignty over the entire universe. This evil entity also went into retreat and meditation to expand its power, though later than the Jade Emperor did. He passed through 3,000 trials, each trial lasting about 3 million years. After its final trial, it felt confident that no one could defeat it. It re-entered the world and recruited an army of demons with the purpose of attacking heaven. The immortals, being aware of the threat, gathered themselves and prepared for war. The gods were unable to stop the powerful demon, and it defeated them all.
The Jade Emperor finished his cultivation during this war. When he was changing the land to make it more livable for men and repelling a variety of monsters, he saw an evil glow radiating from heaven and knew something was amiss. He ascended and saw that the evil entity was too powerful to be stopped by the gods. He challenged it, and they fought. Mountains shook, and rivers and seas toppled. He embodies the pinnacle of divine hierarchy, overseeing the balance of moral order, natural phenomena, and the fates of both mortals and immortals, with subordinate gods serving as officials in his heavenly administration. Known for his impartial judgment and role in granting longevity or punishment, the Jade Emperor represents the fusion of imperial authority with supernatural governance in Chinese cosmology. The origins of the Jade Emperor trace back to pre-imperial concepts of Tian (Heaven) as an impersonal cosmic force and Shangdi (Supreme Sovereign) as a high god in ancient Chinese religion, originating from upper ancient folk worship of the Heavenly Emperor. The Jade Emperor is a Taoist deity formally appearing in the Tang and Song periods. His cult was significantly elevated in the Northern Song dynasty when Emperor Zhenzong, seeking to conceal the humiliation of the Chanyuan Alliance (æ¾¶æ¸ä¹ç) in 1005 with the Liao, claimed to dream of a divine messenger transmitting the Jade Emperor's mandate and forged "heavenly books" (å¤©ä¹¦), leading to the bestowal of the title Yuhuang Shangdi, the integration of his worship into state rituals, and his elevation as a key national sacrificial object. In Taoist theology, he is positioned as an assistant to Yuanshi Tianzun (Celestial Worthy of the Primordial Beginning), one of the Three Pure Ones âthe primordial emanations of the Tao âthus linking him to the religion's philosophical core while emphasizing his administrative duties over metaphysical abstraction. This development highlights the syncretic nature of Chinese religion, blending indigenous animism, Confucian hierarchy, and Taoist cosmology. Depicted in art and literature as a bearded elder in imperial robes seated on a throne, often with attendants like the Thunder God or the Four Heavenly Kings, the Jade Emperor symbolizes ultimate justice and harmony, intervening in myths to resolve chaos, such as quelling rebellions by deities or allocating the Chinese zodiac through legendary races. His annual birthday festival on the ninth day of the first lunar month attracts large crowds to temples, especially in Taiwan and southern China, where rituals involve incense, prayers, and theatrical performances to seek blessings for prosperity and protection. As a pan-Chinese figure transcending strict Taoist boundaries, he influences daily folk practices, from household altars reporting to him via the Kitchen God to grand pilgrimages, underscoring his enduring role in maintaining the interconnected realms of heaven, earth, and the underworld.
